deep.reconstruction:
This page is the opening of a lecture course (Vorlesungen) on elliptic and Abelian functions. It is not a research computation.

(1) Introductory prose. The subject is defined as the theory of elliptic and Abelian functions, i.e. functions arising from the integration of algebraic differentials. The rise of the theory since Abel and Jacobi is said to be due mainly to the introduction of the imaginary. Therefore the general properties of functions of a variable (complex) argument must form the foundation of the investigations. Riemann proposes to go straight to these general properties and not to dwell on the historical development. A margin note says that through the work of Abel and Jacobi the subject has become a theory reaching into all parts of mathematics. A second note, 'Gang der Untersuchungen', concerns the course of the investigation. The bibliographic note points students to Dirichlet's memorial address on C. G. J. Jacobi of 1 July 1852 (Abhandlungen der Berliner Akademie), reprinted in Grunert's Archiv der Mathematik, Theil 22. That volume dates from 1854, so the lecture is from about 1855 or later.

(2) Mathematical part, 'Functionen mit veränderlichem/complexem Argument'.
- Set z = x + i y with i = sqrt(-1), shown as a point with abscissa x and ordinate y.
- Let w = f(z) = u + i v. Then dw = f'(z) dz.
- Varying only x (dz = dx) gives d_x w = f'(z) dx.
- Varying only y (dz = i dy) gives d_y w = f'(z) i dy.
- Hence ∂w/∂x = f'(z) and ∂w/∂y = i f'(z). Eliminating f'(z) gives the complex Cauchy–Riemann equation ∂w/∂y = i ∂w/∂x.
- Implicit step (mine): splitting into real and imaginary parts gives u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x.

The next page continues the argument the other way. Starting from w = φ(x,y) and substituting x = z - iy, the condition ∂w/∂y = i ∂w/∂x is equivalent to w depending on z alone. That page also gives dw = (∂w/∂x)(dx + i dy). This is exactly the definition of a complex function from Riemann's 1851 dissertation.
errors: No mathematical errors. The final line is written as i ∂w/∂x = ∂w/∂y in the transcription; the image appears to show an extra stroke or an i before the right-hand fraction, possibly a correction. The correct relation, ∂w/∂y = i ∂w/∂x, follows from the two preceding lines and is the one used on the next page.

The margin sentence 'ist die Lehre ... zu einer Theorie, welche in alle Theile der Mathematik eingreift' lacks its verb (e.g. 'erhoben/geworden'). This is a stylistic draft slip, not a mathematical one.

results.what: For w = f(z), z = x+iy: ∂w/∂x = f'(z), ∂w/∂y = i f'(z), hence ∂w/∂y = i ∂w/∂x
results.usually_credited_to: d'Alembert (1752), Euler (1777), Cauchy (1814/1825); adopted as the definition of a complex function by Riemann (Inauguraldissertation 1851)

results.what: Programmatic statement that the theory of Abelian functions must be founded on the general theory of functions of a complex variable
results.modern_name: Riemann's function-theoretic approach to Abelian integrals
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (Theorie der Abel'schen Functionen, 1857, and his lectures)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the standard opening of Riemann's lectures on Abelian functions. It contains historical remarks, a literature reference (Dirichlet's 1852 Jacobi memorial address) and the Cauchy–Riemann derivation that Riemann himself published in 1851. The only interest is biographical and pedagogical, e.g. dating the course to after 1854 via Grunert's Archiv Th. 22.

checkable.asserts: Equals 0: the complex Cauchy–Riemann relation ∂w/∂y = i ∂w/∂x for w = z^3.
Equals 0 for an arbitrary differentiable f, via the chain rule ∂/∂y f(x+iy) = i f'(z).

Heading 'Functionen mit veränderlichem[?] Argument': the word may be 'complexem' or 'veränderlichem'; the image is ambiguous.
Last formula: the image appears to read 'i ∂w/∂x = ∂w/∂y', possibly with a stray or crossed i before the right-hand fraction; the intended relation is ∂w/∂y = i ∂w/∂x.
